question.text: When do most crashes at traffic signals happen, and what does that mean when your light turns green?

answer.text: Most crashes at traffic signals happen in the first few seconds after the light changes, so take care when moving off on a fresh green.

teaching.text: The danger is the change itself, so a fresh green calls for a careful start rather than a fast one. Remember: fresh green, careful start.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most crashes at traffic signals happen in the first few seconds after the light changes, so take care when moving off on a fresh green.

question.text: A green light turns yellow as you approach. What should you do, and what if you are already in the intersection?

answer.text: When a yellow light follows a green, stop before the intersection unless you are too close to stop safely, and if the light changes while you are already in the intersection, continue through with caution.

teaching.text: Where you are decides it: with room to stop you stop, and if you are already inside you carry on with caution. Remember: stop unless too close.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a yellow light follows a green, stop before the intersection unless you are too close to stop safely, and if the light changes while you are already in the intersection, continue through with caution.

question.text: What is a stale green, and what should you expect from it?

answer.text: A stale green is a light that has already been green for some time, so be ready for it to turn yellow and then red.

teaching.text: A light that has been green for some time is closer to changing, so approach it ready to stop. Remember: old green turns soon.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A stale green is a light that has already been green for some time, so be ready for it to turn yellow and then red.

question.text: Which signs and lights always require a driver to stop?

answer.text: A driver must stop at a stop sign and at a red light, whether the red is steady or flashing.

teaching.text: A flashing red is still a red light, so it needs the same full stop as a steady red or a stop sign. Remember: red means stop, steady or flashing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must stop at a stop sign and at a red light, whether the red is steady or flashing.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: red means stop, steady or flashing

question.text: Which pedestrians with a cane or a dog must a driver stop for?

answer.text: A driver must stop for a blind pedestrian using a white or metallic cane or a trained guide dog, and for a guide dog instructor who is training a dog.

teaching.text: A white or metallic cane or a trained guide dog tells you the pedestrian is blind, so you stop for them every time. Remember: cane or guide dog, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must stop for a blind pedestrian using a white or metallic cane or a trained guide dog, and for a guide dog instructor who is training a dog.

question.text: When must a driver stop for pedestrians and wheelchair users?

answer.text: A driver must stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk or at an intersection, and for a motorized wheelchair or mobility-assistance device there.

teaching.text: Crosswalk users and wheelchair riders at an intersection come first, so the answer is a full stop. Remember: crosswalk people come first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk or at an intersection, and for a motorized wheelchair or mobility-assistance device there.

question.text: Besides signs and lights, when must a driver stop for an officer or at a yield sign?

answer.text: A driver must also stop when a traffic officer orders it, and at a yield sign when traffic does not allow a safe merge.

teaching.text: A yield sign becomes a stop when there is no safe gap, and an officer's order always means stop. Remember: officer says, yield fails.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must also stop when a traffic officer orders it, and at a yield sign when traffic does not allow a safe merge.

question.text: When must a driver stop when leaving a driveway or approaching a drawbridge?

answer.text: A driver must also stop when coming out of an alley, private driveway or building, and at a bridge span that is about to open for boats.

teaching.text: Leaving a driveway, alley or building, and reaching a bridge about to open, both call for a full stop. Remember: exit driveways, opening bridges.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must also stop when coming out of an alley, private driveway or building, and at a bridge span that is about to open for boats.

question.text: What kinds of warnings can mark a railroad crossing?

answer.text: Railroad crossing warnings can include advance-warning signs, pavement markings, flashing red lights, gates with or without flashing lights, ringing bells and flag signals.

teaching.text: Warnings range from signs and pavement markings on the approach to lights, gates, bells and flags at the crossing. Remember: signs, lights, gates, bells.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Railroad crossing warnings can include advance-warning signs, pavement markings, flashing red lights, gates with or without flashing lights, ringing bells and flag signals.

question.text: How far from a railroad crossing must you stop when its warnings are active, and which warnings count?

answer.text: Stop at least fifteen feet from a railroad crossing when there are flashing red lights, ringing bells, lowering or lowered gates, or flag signals.

teaching.text: Any one active warning is enough; stop well back from the crossing even before a train is in sight. Remember: fifteen feet from the rails.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stop at least fifteen feet from a railroad crossing when there are flashing red lights, ringing bells, lowering or lowered gates, or flag signals.

question.text: After stopping at an active railroad crossing, when may you cross the tracks?

answer.text: Do not cross the tracks until the gates are up, the bells have stopped ringing and the red lights have stopped flashing.

teaching.text: All three must be over, so a gate that is only starting to rise is not yet permission to cross. Remember: gates up, bells quiet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not cross the tracks until the gates are up, the bells have stopped ringing and the red lights have stopped flashing.

question.text: How much distance does a fast train need to stop, and what does that mean for drivers?

answer.text: Most trains moving at sixty miles per hour or more need over a mile to stop, so never race a train.

teaching.text: A train cannot stop in time for you, so the only safe choice is to wait for it. Remember: mile to stop, never race.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most trains moving at sixty miles per hour or more need over a mile to stop, so never race a train.

question.text: Which vehicles must always stop at railroad crossings, and how should you drive behind them?

answer.text: School buses, buses and vehicles carrying hazardous materials must always stop at railroad crossings, so be ready to stop behind them even when no train is signaled.

teaching.text: Their stop is routine at every crossing, so expect it and leave room behind them. Remember: buses always stop at tracks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: School buses, buses and vehicles carrying hazardous materials must always stop at railroad crossings, so be ready to stop behind them even when no train is signaled.

question.text: What should you do about stopping on railroad tracks, and what if the warnings start while you are on them?

answer.text: Never stop on railroad tracks; make sure there is room to get fully across, and if the warning devices start while you are on the tracks, keep going to the other side.

teaching.text: Check for room on the far side before you start across; once on the tracks, the way out is forward. Remember: never stop on rails.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never stop on railroad tracks; make sure there is room to get fully across, and if the warning devices start while you are on the tracks, keep going to the other side.

question.text: When must a driver stop for a school bus?

answer.text: A driver must stop when a school bus is picking up or dropping off children or has its red lights flashing.

teaching.text: Children getting on or off are reason enough to stop, even if the bus lights are not working. Remember: children boarding means stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver must stop when a school bus is picking up or dropping off children or has its red lights flashing.

question.text: What lights does a school bus use when stopping, and why should drivers behind it not rely on them?

answer.text: School buses turn on yellow or amber lights before stopping and red lights once stopped, but drivers behind a bus should not rely on those lights because they could be broken.

teaching.text: Use the lights as a warning, not as a guarantee, and watch for the children themselves. Remember: bus lights can fail.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: School buses turn on yellow or amber lights before stopping and red lights once stopped, but drivers behind a bus should not rely on those lights because they could be broken.

question.text: How far from a school bus with flashing red lights must you stop, and on which kinds of roads?

answer.text: For a school bus with flashing red lights, stop at least twenty-five feet away on a two-lane road, on a multi-lane highway whose lanes are separated only by lines, or on a privately maintained road.

teaching.text: Painted lines are not a median, so traffic on those roads makes the full stop. Remember: twenty-five feet, two-lane stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a school bus with flashing red lights, stop at least twenty-five feet away on a two-lane road, on a multi-lane highway whose lanes are separated only by lines, or on a privately maintained road.

question.text: On a dual-lane highway, what do you do when a stopped school bus is across a safety island or raised median?

answer.text: On a dual-lane highway where you are on the other side of a safety island or raised median from a stopped school bus, slow to ten miles per hour

teaching.text: The median replaces the full stop with a crawl, not with your normal speed. Remember: median means slow to ten.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a dual-lane highway where you are on the other side of a safety island or raised median from a stopped school bus, slow to ten miles per hour

question.text: How may you pass a school bus stopped directly in front of a school to load or unload?

answer.text: When a school bus has stopped directly in front of a school to load or unload, you may pass it from either direction at no more than ten miles per hour

teaching.text: At the school building itself you may pass from either direction, but only at a crawl. Remember: school front, ten max.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a school bus has stopped directly in front of a school to load or unload, you may pass it from either direction at no more than ten miles per hour

question.text: Which two school bus situations each carry a ten miles per hour rule?

answer.text: Two separate ten miles per hour rules apply to school buses: slow to ten miles per hour when you are across a safety island or raised median on a dual-lane highway, and pass at no more than ten miles per hour when the bus is stopped directly in front of a school.

teaching.text: Same speed, different trigger: a median on a dual-lane highway, or a bus parked at the school. Remember: median slow, school-front pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two separate ten miles per hour rules apply to school buses: slow to ten miles per hour when you are across a safety island or raised median on a dual-lane highway, and pass at no more than ten miles per hour when the bus is stopped directly in front of a school.

question.text: After stopping for a school bus, when may you move on, and what must you still watch for?

answer.text: After stopping for a school bus, move on only once its signals are off, and even then watch for children and people with developmental disabilities.

teaching.text: The signals going off ends the stop, but children and people with developmental disabilities may still be near. Remember: signals off, still watch.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After stopping for a school bus, move on only once its signals are off, and even then watch for children and people with developmental disabilities.

question.text: What must you do for an ice cream or frozen dessert truck with flashing red lights and a stop arm?

answer.text: For an ice cream or frozen dessert truck showing flashing red lights and a stop signal arm, yield to anyone crossing to or from it, stop, and then pass at no more than fifteen miles per hour

teaching.text: The dessert truck limit is fifteen, a little higher than the ten used for school buses. Remember: dessert truck, then fifteen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For an ice cream or frozen dessert truck showing flashing red lights and a stop signal arm, yield to anyone crossing to or from it, stop, and then pass at no more than fifteen miles per hour

question.text: Must a driver on the far side of a safety island or raised median stop for a frozen dessert truck?

answer.text: A driver on the far side of a safety island or raised median on a dual highway does not have to stop for a frozen dessert truck.

teaching.text: Across a median, a school bus still means slowing to ten, but a dessert truck needs no stop at all. Remember: median skips the truck.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver on the far side of a safety island or raised median on a dual highway does not have to stop for a frozen dessert truck.

question.text: What do you do when an emergency vehicle uses its siren or flashing lights, and how far back must you stay?

answer.text: When an emergency vehicle uses its siren or flashing red or blue lights, steer to the far right, stop and let it pass, then stay at least three hundred feet behind any signaling emergency vehicle.

teaching.text: Get out of the way first, then hang well back once it has passed. Remember: pull right, three hundred back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When an emergency vehicle uses its siren or flashing red or blue lights, steer to the far right, stop and let it pass, then stay at least three hundred feet behind any signaling emergency vehicle.

question.text: Which emergency vehicles use red lights, and which use blue lights?

answer.text: Police cars, fire trucks, ambulances and other emergency vehicles use sirens and red lights, while private vehicles of volunteer fire and rescue squad members answering a call, with emergency vehicle identification, use blue lights.

teaching.text: Blue lights on a private car still mean a volunteer responder on a call, so yield just as you would to red. Remember: blue means volunteer responders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Police cars, fire trucks, ambulances and other emergency vehicles use sirens and red lights, while private vehicles of volunteer fire and rescue squad members answering a call, with emergency vehicle identification, use blue lights.

question.text: What are the parking and fire hose rules around a fire department vehicle in service?

answer.text: Never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service, and never drive over a fire hose unless a fire, rescue or police official tells you to.

teaching.text: Only a fire, rescue or police officer in charge can wave you over a hose, never your own judgment. Remember: two hundred feet, skip hoses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service, and never drive over a fire hose unless a fire, rescue or police official tells you to.

question.text: Which two emergency-vehicle distances are easy to swap, and what are they?

answer.text: Two emergency-vehicle distances are easy to swap: stay at least three hundred feet behind a signaling emergency vehicle, and never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service.

teaching.text: Follow three, park two: following distance is the bigger number. Remember: follow three, park two.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two emergency-vehicle distances are easy to swap: stay at least three hundred feet behind a signaling emergency vehicle, and never park within two hundred feet of a fire department vehicle in service.

question.text: What does the Move Over law require when you approach a stopped emergency or service vehicle?

answer.text: The Move Over law requires moving into a lane not next to a stopped emergency, tow, highway maintenance or other service vehicle showing flashing lights, or a stopped vehicle using hazard lights, flares or reflective triangles, when safety and traffic allow.

teaching.text: The law covers tow and service vehicles and cars with hazard lights or flares, not only police and ambulances. Remember: give stopped helpers a lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The Move Over law requires moving into a lane not next to a stopped emergency, tow, highway maintenance or other service vehicle showing flashing lights, or a stopped vehicle using hazard lights, flares or reflective triangles, when safety and traffic allow.

question.text: Under the Move Over law, what do you do if moving over is impossible, illegal or unsafe?

answer.text: If moving over is impossible, illegal or unsafe, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit and be ready to stop.

teaching.text: When a lane change is unsafe, slowing down is how you still obey the law. Remember: cannot move? slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If moving over is impossible, illegal or unsafe, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit and be ready to stop.

question.text: What penalties can a Move Over violation bring?

answer.text: A Move Over violation carries a fine of one hundred dollars to five hundred, dollars and three or more convictions can also bring motor vehicle points.

teaching.text: Fines apply from the first violation, and repeat convictions can add points on top. Remember: fines first, then points.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A Move Over violation carries a fine of one hundred dollars to five hundred, dollars and three or more convictions can also bring motor vehicle points.

question.text: What should you do when emergency lights appear behind you?

answer.text: When emergency lights appear behind you, signal, slow down and move promptly to the right shoulder or another safe place.

teaching.text: Signal first so the officer knows you are pulling over, then move promptly to a safe spot. Remember: signal, slow, shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When emergency lights appear behind you, signal, slow down and move promptly to the right shoulder or another safe place.

question.text: Once a police officer has stopped you, what should you do inside the vehicle?

answer.text: During a police stop, put the vehicle in park, stay inside unless told otherwise, roll down the window, switch on the interior light at night and keep your hands visible, ideally on the steering wheel.

teaching.text: Every step makes you easy to see and predictable, which keeps the stop calm. Remember: park, window, light, hands.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: During a police stop, put the vehicle in park, stay inside unless told otherwise, roll down the window, switch on the interior light at night and keep your hands visible, ideally on the steering wheel.

question.text: How should you behave during a police stop, and what about reaching for documents?

answer.text: During a police stop, turn the music down, avoid sudden movements, and do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, saying first what you are about to do.

teaching.text: Announce before you move, and reach only once you are told to. Remember: calm, quiet, announce moves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: During a police stop, turn the music down, avoid sudden movements, and do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, saying first what you are about to do.

question.text: When should interior overhead lights be used while driving or when stopped?

answer.text: Interior overhead lights should be used only briefly while driving, or when a police officer asks you to light up the inside of a stopped vehicle.

teaching.text: The interior light is for brief use while driving, or for lighting up the car when an officer asks. Remember: cabin light only briefly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Interior overhead lights should be used only briefly while driving, or when a police officer asks you to light up the inside of a stopped vehicle.

question.text: Which documents must New Jersey drivers show at a traffic stop?

answer.text: At a traffic stop, New Jersey drivers must show a valid driver license, the vehicle registration and proof of insurance.

teaching.text: All three are required: the license, the registration and the insurance proof. Remember: license, registration, insurance.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a traffic stop, New Jersey drivers must show a valid driver license, the vehicle registration and proof of insurance.

question.text: How should you respond to an officer's instructions during a stop?

answer.text: Follow the officer's instructions, including stepping out of the vehicle if asked, and politely ask for an instruction to be repeated if it is unclear.

teaching.text: Stepping out is part of following instructions, and asking for a repeat is better than guessing. Remember: follow, ask politely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Follow the officer's instructions, including stepping out of the vehicle if asked, and politely ask for an instruction to be repeated if it is unclear.

question.text: If you disagree with a police stop, what should you do?

answer.text: If you disagree with a stop, do not argue at the roadside; you can contest the ticket later in court or file a complaint with the law enforcement agency.

teaching.text: Save the argument for court or a formal complaint, never the roadside. Remember: argue in court, not roadside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you disagree with a stop, do not argue at the roadside; you can contest the ticket later in court or file a complaint with the law enforcement agency.

question.text: During which hours are headlights required?

answer.text: Headlights are required from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise.

teaching.text: The window starts after sunset and ends before sunrise, so dusk and dawn count. Remember: half hour each side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are required from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise.

question.text: Besides the time of day, when else are headlights required?

answer.text: Headlights are also required whenever visibility is five hundred feet or less, whenever the windshield wipers are in use, and in fog, mist, smoke or anything else that cuts visibility.

teaching.text: Conditions add to the clock: wipers on means headlights on, even at midday. Remember: wipers on, lights on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are also required whenever visibility is five hundred feet or less, whenever the windshield wipers are in use, and in fog, mist, smoke or anything else that cuts visibility.

question.text: Can parking lights or auxiliary lights stand in for headlights when headlights are required?

answer.text: Parking lights or auxiliary lights may not legally take the place of headlights when headlights are required.

teaching.text: Parking lights and auxiliary lights are add-ons, never substitutes for headlights. Remember: parking lights never replace headlights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking lights or auxiliary lights may not legally take the place of headlights when headlights are required.

question.text: What are fog lights, and how may they be used?

answer.text: Fog lights are auxiliary lights that may be used together with low beams to light the road ahead in foggy weather.

teaching.text: Fog lights add to low beams; they never stand in for headlights. Remember: fog lights with low beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Fog lights are auxiliary lights that may be used together with low beams to light the road ahead in foggy weather.

question.text: When may you use high beams, and when must you switch them off?

answer.text: Use high beams only in open country with no traffic in sight, and switch them off when another vehicle approaches or when you are following one.

teaching.text: Open country and no traffic in sight are both needed; a car ahead or approaching means low beams. Remember: open country only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use high beams only in open country with no traffic in sight, and switch them off when another vehicle approaches or when you are following one.

question.text: When are high beams used, and when are low beams used?

answer.text: High beams are for open country with no traffic in sight, while low beams are for city driving, heavier traffic, following another vehicle and meeting oncoming vehicles.

teaching.text: Low beams are the default for town, traffic, following and meeting; high beams are the exception. Remember: high for empty, low otherwise.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High beams are for open country with no traffic in sight, while low beams are for city driving, heavier traffic, following another vehicle and meeting oncoming vehicles.

question.text: Why can bright beams blind other drivers at night?

answer.text: At night the pupils are dilated, and bright beams can blind other drivers for a moment by making their pupils constrict.

teaching.text: Wide-open night pupils snap smaller under a bright beam, and that is what blinds a driver for a moment. Remember: wide pupils, sudden glare.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night the pupils are dilated, and bright beams can blind other drivers for a moment by making their pupils constrict.

question.text: How long can it take to recover from oncoming high-beam glare, and how far does a car travel meanwhile?

answer.text: Recovering from the glare of oncoming high beams can take three to five seconds, and at fifty miles per hour a driver covers the length of a football field in that blind time.

teaching.text: Glare costs real distance: at fifty miles per hour you can travel a football field while still dazzled. Remember: football field of blindness.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Recovering from the glare of oncoming high beams can take three to five seconds, and at fifty miles per hour a driver covers the length of a football field in that blind time.

question.text: What should you do if an oncoming driver has high beams on?

answer.text: If an oncoming driver has high beams on, look toward the right side of the road until it passes, and never flash your own high beams back.

teaching.text: Shift your eyes to the right edge until the car passes, and never answer with your own high beams. Remember: eyes right, no flashback.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming driver has high beams on, look toward the right side of the road until it passes, and never flash your own high beams back.

question.text: When do taillights come on and grow brighter?

answer.text: Taillights come on with the headlights and parking lights and grow brighter when the brakes are applied; in daylight they also light up when braking.

teaching.text: Taillights are on with the headlights and parking lights, and the brakes make them brighter. Remember: brakes brighten the taillights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Taillights come on with the headlights and parking lights and grow brighter when the brakes are applied; in daylight they also light up when braking.

question.text: How bright should dashboard lights be?

answer.text: Keep dashboard lights dim enough to avoid glare but bright enough to read the dials.

teaching.text: Too bright causes glare and too dim hides the dials, so aim for the middle. Remember: dim but readable.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep dashboard lights dim enough to avoid glare but bright enough to read the dials.

question.text: When may spotlights and hazard flashers be used?

answer.text: Spotlights and hazard flashers are for emergencies only, and spotlights may never be used for driving.

teaching.text: A spotlight may seem useful on a dark road, but it is for emergencies only and never a driving light. Remember: emergencies only, never drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Spotlights and hazard flashers are for emergencies only, and spotlights may never be used for driving.

question.text: Where must parked vehicles show parking lights?

answer.text: Parking lights are required on vehicles parked anywhere other than business or residential zones.

teaching.text: This is a parked-car rule, separate from the rule that parking lights cannot replace headlights while driving. Remember: outside town zones, parking lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking lights are required on vehicles parked anywhere other than business or residential zones.

question.text: How far from the curb may a vehicle legally be parked?

answer.text: Parking a vehicle more than six inches from the curb is illegal.

teaching.text: Pull in close, because anything more than six inches from the curb breaks the rule. Remember: six inches, no more.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking a vehicle more than six inches from the curb is illegal.

question.text: How close to a fire hydrant may you park?

answer.text: Do not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant.

teaching.text: The hydrant is the smallest parking distance, ten feet, not the twenty used for fire stations. Remember: ten feet for hydrants.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant.

question.text: How close to a crosswalk at an intersection may you park?

answer.text: Do not park within twenty-five feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, except at alleys.

teaching.text: The crosswalk distance sits between the hydrant and the stop sign distances. Remember: twenty-five from crosswalks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within twenty-five feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, except at alleys.

question.text: How close to a railroad crossing or a stop sign may you park?

answer.text: Do not park within fifty feet of a railroad crossing or within fifty feet of a stop sign.

teaching.text: Railroad crossings and stop signs share one number, so learn them as a pair. Remember: fifty for rails and stops.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within fifty feet of a railroad crossing or within fifty feet of a stop sign.

question.text: What are the parking distances for a fire station driveway on your side and across the street?

answer.text: Do not park within twenty feet of a fire station driveway, or within seventy-five feet of the entrance on the opposite side of the street.

teaching.text: Near side twenty, far side seventy-five; the distance is larger across the street. Remember: twenty near, seventy-five across.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within twenty feet of a fire station driveway, or within seventy-five feet of the entrance on the opposite side of the street.

question.text: Which two no-parking rules both use a distance of twenty feet?

answer.text: Two different twenty-foot no-parking rules exist: within twenty feet of the end of a pedestrian safety zone, and within twenty feet of a fire station driveway entrance.

teaching.text: Twenty feet appears twice, once for a fire station driveway and once for a pedestrian safety zone end. Remember: twin twenty-foot zones.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two different twenty-foot no-parking rules exist: within twenty feet of the end of a pedestrian safety zone, and within twenty feet of a fire station driveway entrance.

question.text: Where may you never stop or park?

answer.text: Never stop or park in a crosswalk, on a sidewalk, in a bus stop zone, in front of a driveway, inside an intersection, on an interstate, on a bridge, elevated roadway or in a tunnel, next to a car already parked at the curb, or in a disability space without authorization.

teaching.text: These spots are banned for stopping as well as parking, so distance from a sign does not matter there. Remember: no tunnels, bridges, crosswalks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never stop or park in a crosswalk, on a sidewalk, in a bus stop zone, in front of a driveway, inside an intersection, on an interstate, on a bridge, elevated roadway or in a tunnel, next to a car already parked at the curb, or in a disability space without authorization.

question.text: What should you check before opening the driver-side door, and where should passengers get out?

answer.text: Before opening the driver-side door, check for traffic and for hard-to-see bicycles and mopeds, because a driver who opens a door into traffic may be liable for the crash; passengers should get out on the curb side.

teaching.text: Looking back before opening protects cyclists, and the curb side keeps passengers out of traffic. Remember: look back before opening.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before opening the driver-side door, check for traffic and for hard-to-see bicycles and mopeds, because a driver who opens a door into traffic may be liable for the crash; passengers should get out on the curb side.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle has mechanical trouble or another emergency?

answer.text: If your vehicle has mechanical trouble or another emergency, stop on the right shoulder and turn on the emergency flashers.

teaching.text: A breakdown stop belongs on the right shoulder, with flashers telling others why you are there. Remember: shoulder right, flashers on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle has mechanical trouble or another emergency, stop on the right shoulder and turn on the emergency flashers.

question.text: What is the rule on handheld and hands-free phones while driving on a public road?

answer.text: Using a handheld phone or texting device while driving on any public road is a primary offense, while a hands-free phone is legal but strongly discouraged.

teaching.text: Handheld use is a violation on its own; hands-free is allowed for most drivers but still discouraged. Remember: hands-free legal, handheld banned.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Using a handheld phone or texting device while driving on any public road is a primary offense, while a hands-free phone is legal but strongly discouraged.

question.text: When may a driver use a handheld phone while driving, and how?

answer.text: A handheld phone may be used only in an emergency such as a fire, a traffic crash, a serious road hazard, a medical emergency or a hazardous material emergency, and one hand must stay on the wheel.

teaching.text: The exception is narrow: a true emergency, and still one hand on the wheel. Remember: emergency only, hand on wheel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A handheld phone may be used only in an emergency such as a fire, a traffic crash, a serious road hazard, a medical emergency or a hazardous material emergency, and one hand must stay on the wheel.

question.text: How might a driver prove that a handheld phone was used legally in an emergency?

answer.text: To prove a handheld phone was used legally in an emergency, a driver may have to provide testimony or written statements from the authorities, or phone records.

teaching.text: Be ready to back up an emergency claim with testimony, statements from authorities or phone records. Remember: prove it with records.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To prove a handheld phone was used legally in an emergency, a driver may have to provide testimony or written statements from the authorities, or phone records.

question.text: What fines and other penalties apply to handheld phone offenses?

answer.text: Handheld phone fines are two hundred dollars to four hundred dollars for a first offense, four hundred dollars to six hundred dollars for a second within ten years, and six hundred dollars to eight hundred dollars for a third or later offense, which also brings three points and possibly a ninety-day suspension.

teaching.text: Each repeat offense moves you into a higher fine range, and a third adds points and a possible suspension. Remember: fines climb each offense.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Handheld phone fines are two hundred dollars to four hundred dollars for a first offense, four hundred dollars to six hundred dollars for a second within ten years, and six hundred dollars to eight hundred dollars for a third or later offense, which also brings three points and possibly a ninety-day suspension.

question.text: What phone and device rule applies to a GDL holder while driving?

answer.text: A GDL holder may not use a handheld or hands-free phone, or any other handheld electronic device, while driving.

teaching.text: A GDL holder gets no phone at all while driving, not even hands-free. Remember: GDL means no phone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A GDL holder may not use a handheld or hands-free phone, or any other handheld electronic device, while driving.

question.text: What phone rule applies to a school bus driver while driving the bus?

answer.text: A school bus driver may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving the bus, except in an emergency or when parked in a safe place off the highway.

teaching.text: Unlike a GDL holder, a school bus driver has two exceptions: an emergency, or parked safely off the highway. Remember: bus drivers park first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A school bus driver may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving the bus, except in an emergency or when parked in a safe place off the highway.

question.text: What does Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law do about illegal cell phone use?

answer.text: Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law, enacted in two thousand twelve, treats illegal cell phone use while driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide and assault by auto statutes.

teaching.text: Under this law, illegal phone use can be treated as recklessness in the most serious crash cases. Remember: phone crash means recklessness.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law, enacted in two thousand twelve, treats illegal cell phone use while driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide and assault by auto statutes.

question.text: What are the penalties for throwing trash or objects from a vehicle?

answer.text: Throwing trash from a moving or parked vehicle is illegal, throwing dangerous objects onto a roadway can bring fines of up to one thousand, dollars and littering from a moving vehicle can cost the driver the license.

teaching.text: The driver can lose the license for littering from a moving vehicle, so the penalty goes beyond a fine. Remember: toss trash, risk license.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Throwing trash from a moving or parked vehicle is illegal, throwing dangerous objects onto a roadway can bring fines of up to one thousand, dollars and littering from a moving vehicle can cost the driver the license.

question.text: What must you do with trash, debris or rubbish you carry in a vehicle?

answer.text: Any trash, debris or rubbish carried in a vehicle must be covered so it cannot litter the road.

teaching.text: Covering the load is part of the same rule against littering the road. Remember: cover the load.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Any trash, debris or rubbish carried in a vehicle must be covered so it cannot litter the road.

hooks_spoken: Take care on a fresh green, expect a stale green to change, and stop on yellow unless you are too close to stop safely.
Stop at stop signs and every red light, for blind pedestrians and crosswalk pedestrians, for officers, at a yield sign with no safe merge, leaving driveways and at an opening bridge.

Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: When a crossing signals, stop at least fifteen feet back and wait until the gates are up, the bells stop and the red lights stop flashing.
A fast train needs over a mile to stop, buses and hazardous loads always stop, and you never stop on the tracks.

hooks_spoken: Stop at least twenty-five feet from a bus with flashing reds, do not rely on its lights, and go only once the signals are off.
Ten miles per hour across a median or past a school-front bus; stop for a dessert truck, then pass at fifteen, unless a median separates you.

hooks_spoken: Pull right and stop for sirens, then follow three hundred feet back, and never park within two hundred feet of a working fire vehicle.
Red lights mean police, fire or ambulance; blue lights mean volunteer responders in their own cars.
Move over a lane for stopped helpers, slow down if you cannot, and expect fines and possible points for ignoring the rule.

hooks_spoken: Signal and pull to the right shoulder, park, lower the window, light the cabin at night and keep your hands visible on the wheel.

hooks_spoken: Headlights go on from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and also with wipers, fog or short visibility; parking lights never stand in.
High beams belong only on empty open roads; glare can blind you for seconds, so look right and never flash back.
Taillights brighten when you brake, dashboard lights stay dim but readable, and spotlights and flashers are for emergencies.

hooks_spoken: Park within six inches of the curb, ten feet from a hydrant, twenty-five from a crosswalk and fifty from a crossing or stop sign.
Fire station driveways need twenty feet on your side and seventy-five across the street, a safety zone end also needs twenty, and a breakdown goes on the right shoulder with flashers on.
Never park in a tunnel, on a bridge or beside a parked car, show parking lights outside business or residential zones, and check for bikes before opening your door.
